outcomes.description: Calculate redshift, lensing, orbital effects, linearized gravitational waves and expansion predictions with observational limitations.
Derive Einstein equations from a bounded variational treatment and solve symmetric vacuum and cosmological examples.
Construct Lorentzian metrics, stress-energy tensors, covariant conservation and geodesic observables with explicit coordinate conventions.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Measurement and Experimental Reasoning
decks.description: Produce traceable physical measurements.

includes: Calibration, units, dimensional analysis, uncertainty and experimental decisions

practice: Measure a physical constant with two methods and reconcile discrepancies through calibration and an uncertainty budget.

outcomes.description: Design controls and justify measurement, safety and reporting choices against competing accuracy, cost and risk constraints.
Select ranges, calibrate elementary sensors and record measurements with units, resolution and traceable procedures.
Distinguish random and systematic errors; propagate independent uncertainties by taught sensitivity and root-sum-square rules.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Newtonian Mechanics
decks.description: Predict classical motion from forces and conservation.

includes: Newtonian particles, conservation laws, rigid rotation and gravitation

practice: Predict and experimentally compare a rolling or orbital motion, checking forces, conservation and limiting cases.

outcomes.description: Calculate work, energy, momentum, collisions and central gravitational trajectories with justified conservation assumptions.
Construct free-body diagrams and solve particle motion in Cartesian and plane-polar coordinates using Newton laws.
Calculate centers of mass, moments of inertia, torque, angular momentum and simple rigid-body rotation.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Modern Physics Foundations
decks.description: Use accessible relativistic and quantum models.

includes: Special relativity, photon and matter-wave models, atomic spectra and radioactive evidence
excludes: Quantum operator theory and general relativity

practice: Infer hidden energies or lifetimes from unfamiliar spectral and decay observations and solve a relativistic collision.

outcomes.description: Interpret atomic spectra, quantized energy diagrams and exponential radioactive decay while identifying classical-model failures.
Use explicitly defined wavelength, frequency, photon and de Broglie relations to predict thresholds and interference scales.
Calculate Lorentz transformations, spacetime intervals and relativistic energy-momentum conservation in one-dimensional events.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Nuclear and Particle Physics
decks.description: Infer subatomic processes from energies and detector evidence.

includes: Nuclear structure, reactions, particle families, relativistic kinematics and radiation detection

practice: Analyze an archived decay or collision dataset, reconstruct energies and quantify background, efficiency and model ambiguity.

outcomes.description: Explain radiation-matter interactions and calibrate detector spectra, efficiencies, backgrounds and counting-based significance.
Calculate binding, decay, reaction energetics and elementary cross sections using liquid-drop, shell and tunneling models.
Classify particles and interactions and calculate threshold and invariant-mass kinematics with conservation and selection rules.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Optical Physics and Photonics
decks.description: Analyze advanced optical propagation and instruments.

includes: Gaussian propagation, Fourier optics, coherence, laser physics and optical detection

practice: Design a laser-based imaging or sensing system and validate propagation, resolution and noise predictions with safe data or apparatus.

outcomes.description: Analyze coherence, interferometric sensing, imaging resolution and photodetection noise; design an optical measurement chain.
Calculate transition-driven absorption, stimulated emission and laser thresholds using rate equations and bounded nonlinear optical models.
Derive paraxial propagation, Gaussian beams, resonator stability and Fourier-optical transfer functions.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Plasma Physics
decks.description: Connect particle, fluid and kinetic plasma descriptions.

includes: Charged-particle motion, screening, plasma waves, magnetohydrodynamics and kinetic theory

practice: Compare particle, fluid and kinetic predictions for a plasma-wave dataset and justify the regime and stability assumptions.

outcomes.description: Derive plasma-fluid and magnetohydrodynamic models and analyze bounded wave dispersion, equilibrium and instability problems.
Derive Vlasov and elementary collisional descriptions and calculate linear kinetic response and Landau damping with stated contour assumptions.
Calculate charged-particle gyromotion, drifts and adiabatic invariants and identify magnetization and screening scales.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Quantum Field Theory
decks.description: Calculate observables in relativistic quantum field models.

includes: Relativistic fields, quantization, perturbative scattering, renormalization and gauge-theory foundations
excludes: Nonperturbative constructive field theory and quantum gravity

practice: Derive and compute a scattering observable in a specified field theory, documenting gauge, normalization and regularization conventions.

outcomes.description: Derive classical scalar, spinor and gauge field equations and construct canonical and Gaussian path-integral quantization.
Explain gauge symmetry, spontaneous symmetry breaking and Standard Model field content and calculate a bounded electroweak or strong-interaction observable.
Derive propagators and Feynman rules and calculate low-order amplitudes, cross sections and bounded regularization and renormalization examples.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Quantum Many-Body Matter
decks.description: Analyze interacting quantum materials through effective theories.

includes: Second quantization, Green functions, linear response and representative interacting quantum phases

practice: Derive an interacting lattice-model approximation and compare its spectral or transport predictions with exact small-system calculations.

outcomes.description: Analyze representative superconducting, magnetic and topological effective models and distinguish robust predictions from approximation artifacts.
Construct second-quantized lattice Hamiltonians and derive mean-field and elementary quasiparticle approximations.
Calculate correlation and Green functions and derive bounded linear-response and spectral predictions.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Quantum Mechanics
decks.description: Calculate quantum states and observable predictions.

includes: Quantum postulates, wavefunctions, one-dimensional potentials, spin and central-force systems

practice: Solve an unfamiliar piecewise potential and spin-preparation experiment, comparing analytic predictions with numerical eigenvalues.

outcomes.description: Calculate spin measurements and angular-momentum algebra; separate central potentials in spherical coordinates and derive hydrogenic spectra.
Represent pure states with complex vectors and wavefunctions; calculate normalization, observables, uncertainty and unitary evolution.
Solve one-dimensional Schrödinger boundary problems, tunneling and the harmonic oscillator, checking matching and probability current.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Statistical Mechanics
decks.description: Connect microscopic models to thermal observables.

includes: Equilibrium ensembles, partition functions, ideal quantum gases, fluctuations and Monte Carlo sampling

practice: Compare exact and sampled observables for a finite spin model and quantify equilibration and size-dependent uncertainty.

outcomes.description: Derive microcanonical, canonical and grand-canonical predictions and calculate thermodynamic observables and fluctuations from partition functions.
Derive classical, Bose and Fermi occupation laws and calculate ideal-gas, phonon and simple phase-transition behavior.
Implement Metropolis sampling with detailed-balance reasoning and diagnose equilibration, autocorrelation and finite-size effects.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Thermodynamics
decks.description: Analyze equilibrium thermal systems and cycles.

includes: Thermal state variables, ideal gases, heat, work, entropy and thermodynamic potentials
excludes: Microscopic ensembles and mixture chemical potentials

practice: Analyze a nonstandard thermal cycle and compare predicted work and entropy production with supplied measurements.

outcomes.description: Apply first and second laws to engines, refrigerators and irreversible changes; calculate entropy and efficiency bounds.
Use internal energy, enthalpy and free energies to select equilibrium criteria and interpret simple phase transitions.
Define temperature, pressure, state functions and equations of state; calculate heat capacity and quasistatic work.

decks.subject: physics
decks.title: Waves and Introductory Optics
decks.description: Predict oscillatory and wave phenomena.

includes: Forced oscillators, normal modes, wave equations, ray optics, interference and diffraction

practice: Measure resonances and an optical interference pattern, comparing fitted parameters with independently measured geometry.

outcomes.description: Construct paraxial ray images and calculate interference, polarization and scalar far-field diffraction patterns.
Solve damped and driven oscillators and coupled normal modes; calculate resonance and energy transfer.
Derive the one-dimensional string wave equation and calculate traveling, standing and dispersive wave behavior.

scopeIssues: Graduate systems biology and computational neuroscience currently share biology/systems-biology. Its earliest reaction-network and flux-balance tasks unnecessarily require the complete biology/neuroscience and animal-physiology ancestry; these working capabilities need a separate accessible quantitative-cellular destination connected to the neural continuation.

Graduate stochastic-process theory in mathematics/stochastic-processes currently requires numerical methods and differential equations for every learner, although its first measure-theoretic probability and Markov-chain tasks do not need that preparation. A separate probability/process foundation and connected stochastic-calculus continuation are needed.

Undergraduate computational physics in physics/computational-physics imposes optimization and statistical inference on first forward-simulation tasks. The forward simulation and field-solver route should be separated from the inverse-modeling continuation.

chemistry/advanced-inorganic-chemistry promises kinetic discrimination of catalytic mechanisms but does not require chemistry/kinetics or locally teach rate-law derivation and fitting. Its graduate catalytic-inference preparation remains insufficient.

The current inventory does not yet provide independently assessable graduate algebraic geometry or analytic/algebraic number-theory foundations beyond elementary number theory and graduate algebra; these established mathematical continuations remain unfinished.

Established working and graduate foundations for computer vision, robotics/control and information theory are not independently specified. Graphics, classical AI, optimization and signal analysis do not by themselves teach their distinctive inverse-inference, state-estimation and coding methods.
The coverage inventory lacks matching deferred rows for the unfinished mathematical and computing domains identified above; those domains must not be treated as available preparation.
practiceNotes: Recall practice should maintain definitions, representations, assumptions, mechanism steps, diagnostic signatures and method-selection criteria; it does not replace assessed construction or investigation.
Assess proofs through complete arguments and counterexamples; assess programming through executable artifacts, adversarial tests, reproducibility and explanation of complexity or numerical error.

Laboratory and field work requires appropriate facilities, training, supervision and local risk approval. Use safe substitutes or archived data when access is unavailable; this does not certify hands-on competence.
Human-participant studies, identifiable biological data, vertebrate work, environmental sampling and genetic manipulation require applicable consent, authorization and ethics review.
Cybersecurity practice must use owned or explicitly authorized isolated systems. Distributed-system fault injection must not affect operational services.
Radiation, lasers, high voltage, pressure systems, cryogens and hazardous chemicals require specialist supervision and approved procedures; the curriculum does not confer operating authorization.
Biological culture work should use approved low-risk organisms. Clinical reasoning projects use de-identified or synthetic cases and do not authorize diagnosis or treatment.

Provided scientific software may be used only where the contract teaches model specification, inputs, diagnostics and limitations; algorithm implementation and theorem proving are assessed separately when explicitly promised.
Use unfamiliar transfer problems, cumulative projects and delayed reassessment. Preserve laboratory notebooks, code versions, uncertainty budgets and negative results as evidence of competence.
